---
kind: question
title: "No — you multiply by *any* polynomial, not by one from $J[x]$."
---

Fair question, and the whole disagreement is in one word: *generate*.

You built

$$I_{x} = \{\, x\,h(x) : h \in J[x] \,\}$$

— the multiplier taken from $J[x]$. That is not the ideal generated by $J[x]$
and $x$. It is not even an ideal containing $x$: to get $x$ itself out of your
set you would need $h = 1$, and $1 \notin J[x]$, because $1 \notin J$. Your set
does not contain the element you were told to throw in.

**The ideal generated by $J[x]$ together with a polynomial $g$** is the
*smallest* ideal containing both. Write down what you are forced to include:

- every element of $J[x]$;
- $g \cdot h$ for **every** $h \in R[x]$ — absorption says the multiplier is an
  arbitrary polynomial, coefficients unrestricted, so $h = 1$ and $h = 7$ and
  $h = x^{5}$ are all allowed;
- every sum of those.

That set is already an ideal, so it is the one:

$$I_{g} = \{\, a(x) + g(x)h(x) \;:\; a \in J[x],\ h \in R[x] \,\}$$

So no — the coefficients are **not** still limited to $J$. Taking $a = 0$ and
$h = 1$ gives you $g$ itself, and $g$ was chosen outside $J[x]$. Everything in
sight got bigger.

## Exercise 3.26, part 2

Suppose $J$ is a proper prime ideal in an **integral domain** $R$. Show that
$J[x]$ is **not** a maximal proper ideal in $R[x]$ — i.e. produce an ideal $I$
with $J[x] \subsetneq I \subsetneq R[x]$.

### Everything the question below uses

- $R[x]$: polynomials in $x$ with coefficients in $R$; $a_{i}$ is the coefficient of $x^{i}$, and $a_{0}$ the **constant term**.
- $J[x]$: the polynomials **every one of whose coefficients lies in $J$**.
- *Ideal* $I$ of $R[x]$: closed under addition, and **absorbing** — $c \in I$, $r \in R[x]$ $\Rightarrow$ $rc \in I$.
- *Proper*: $I \neq R[x]$; equivalently $1 \notin I$. An ideal containing $1$ contains $r \cdot 1 = r$ for every $r$, so it is everything.
- $I_{g}$, the ideal generated by $J[x]$ and $g$: the set $\{a + gh : a \in J[x],\ h \in R[x]\}$ displayed above.
- Here: $R = \mathbb{Z}$, $J = (3) = $ the multiples of $3$. So $J[x]$ is the polynomials all of whose coefficients are multiples of $3$, and $1 \notin J$.

---

**Your move.** Same two candidates, now with the right notion of generation:

$$g = x \qquad\text{and}\qquad g = 3x + 1$$

Exactly one of $I_{x}$, $I_{3x+1}$ is the whole of $\mathbb{Z}[x]$. Which one —
and write down the choice of $a \in J[x]$ and $h \in \mathbb{Z}[x]$ that puts
$1$ into it.
